subject: Automotive & EVs
title: The Ford Model T
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Ford Model T usable.

hook.text: The Model T didn't just change cars. It changed who could own one—from the rich to everyone.

buildup.text: Ford's assembly line drove the price from $850 in 1908 to $260 by 1925—cheaper than a horse and buggy.

discovery.text: By 1918, half of all cars in America were Model Ts. One single model dominated the entire market.

twist.text: Ford refused to update it. GM introduced yearly model changes and color options, stealing customers.

climax.text: The Model T was finally killed in 1927 after 15 million units. Ford had to shut down for months to retool.

punchline.text: The car that made cars affordable refused to evolve.

quiz.question: Why did the Model T lose to GM?
options: Ford refused to update or add options

details.summary: Henry Ford's Model T, produced from 1908 to 1927, was the car that put the world on wheels, with over 15 million units sold thanks to assembly line production that slashed prices year after year.
details.whyItMatters: The Model T proved that automobiles could be for everyone, not just the wealthy. Its production methods transformed manufacturing and created the modern consumer economy.
takeaways: Its price fell from $850 in 1908 to $260 by the mid-1920s
At peak production, one rolled off the line every 24 seconds
It accounted for half of all cars in the world at one point

faq.question: Why was the Model T so much cheaper than other cars?
faq.answer: Ford's moving assembly line, standardized parts, and relentless efficiency improvements cut production time from 12 hours to 93 minutes per car. He passed the savings on as lower prices to sell more volume.

faq.question: Was the Model T reliable?
faq.answer: Remarkably so for its era. Its simple design meant almost anyone could repair it with basic tools. Parts were standardized and widely available, making the Model T practical for rural owners far from mechanics.
